Yes - the relevant files for the Astrocade hardware are:

for MAME:
src\drivers\astrocde.c for the main driver file (This is where the ROM and
MEMORY defs are)
src\machine\astrocde.c for misc stuff not in the main driver file
src\vidhrdw\astrocde.c for the video emulation
src\sndhrdw\astrocde.c for the sound emulation
src\includes\astrocde.h for any shared includes (not used currently)
src\driver.c for a list of game drivers and descriptions

for MESS, it is very similar:
mess\systems\astrocde.c for the main driver file (This is where the ROM and
MEMORY defs are)
mess\machine\astrocde.c for misc stuff not in the main driver file
mess\vidhrdw\astrocde.c for the video emulation
mess\sndhrdw\astrocde.c for the sound emulation
mess\includes\astrocde.h for any shared includes (not used currently)
mess\system.c for a list of consoles and computers and descriptions

-Frank

INVENTORY [items carried]." If true, then "H" is set to "O", the 
location previously defined in Line 100 ("O=205"). "O=205" means that 
the item is being WORN/USED. "H" variable holds the present location 
of the HELMET.

113 IF K=101 K=O

Line 113 asks if "K=101", then "K=O". "IF K=101" means that "IF 
K=101, then 'K' must equal 101, or the location of the player's 
INVENTORY [items carried]." If true, then "K" is set to "O", the 
location previously defined in Line 100 ("O=205"). "O=205" means that 
the item is being WORN/USED. "K" variable holds the present location 
of the CLOAK.

Line 110 through 113 might be a tad confusing, so please e-mail me 
at: ( dunric@yahoo.com ) with any questions.

114 RETURN

Line 114 RETURNs to the previously issued GOSUB (issued in Line 3 --
> "GOSUB100").

200 E=9;W=16;D=14;V=19;S=5;M=18;H=1;K=9;RETURN

Line 200 sets the beginning locations for the HOBBIT (variable "E"), 
WEREWOLF (variable "W"), DRAGON (variable "D") and VAMPIRE 
(variable "V"). It also assigns beginning room locations to the SWORD 
(variable "S"), ARMOR (variable "M"), HELMET (variable "H") and CLOAK 
(variable "K"). Line 200 then RETURNs to the line that called it 
previously (Line 1).

202 IF E=A E=99

Line 202 asks if "E=A", then "E=99". "E=A" means that the player was 
fighting the HOBBIT (variable "E") in the present room location 
(variable "A"). If so, then move HOBBIT to location 99 (E=99). "99" 
is "nowhere".

203 IF W=A W=99

Line 203 asks if "W=A", then "W=99". "W=A" means that the player was 
fighting the WEREWOLF (variable "W") in the present room location 
(variable "W"). If so, then move WEREWOLF to location 99 (W=99). "99" 
is "nowhere".

204 IF D=A D=99

Line 204 asks if "D=A", then "D=99". "D=A" means that the player was 
fighting the DRAGON (variable "D") in the present room location 
(variable "A"). If so, then move DRAGON to location 99 (D=99). "99" 
is "nowhere".

205 IF V=A V=99;GOTO207

Line 205 asks if "V=A", then "V=99". "V=A" means that the player was 
fighting the VAMPIRE (variable "V") in the present room location 
(variable "A"). If so, then move VAMPIRE to location 99 (V=99), then 
jump to the "Win Game" subroutine in Line 207 (remember that "99" 
is "nowhere"). The object of the game, although not stated within the 
program, is to defeat the vampire. This should probably be stated, in 
either another program or the instructions (if enough RAM permits, of 
course). 

206 GOTO2

Line 206 jumps back up to Line 2, where the main parser begins.

207 PRINT"VAMPIRE DIED!

Line 207 is reached if the player defeats the vampire. If so, the 
message "VAMPIRE DIED!" is displayed, and the program then drops to 
Line 209 below.

209 PRINT"GAME OVER";STOP

Line 209 prints out the "GAME OVER" message. It can be reached if the 
player loses in combat (tested for in Line 97), or if the player 
successfully defeats the vampire (tested for in Line 205).

Lines 210 through 213 check for error conditions, e.g. "bad input" by 
the player.

210 IF C=0 PRINT"SORRY

Line 210 asks is "C=0", then print "SORRY". "C=0" means that the 
command was either "0" (e.g. "nothing"), or the command was not valid 
(e.g. "any number of conditions applied here").

211 IF Z=A PRINT"HOW?

Line 211 asks if "Z=A", then print the message "HOW?". By "Z=A", we 
mean several things: 1) the room the player wishes to visit is not 
valid (e.g. not on the map) 2) the command the player entered does 
not correspond to the verb (e.g. "GET WEREWOLF") or 3) the noun 
entered does not correspond to the situation (e.g. "GET SWORD", when 
the "SWORD" is not located within the present room (variable "A") ).

If you have any questions about Line 211 above, please e-mail me at: 
dunric@yahoo.com

212 IF Z=0 PRINT"SORRY

Line 212 asks if "Z=0", then print the message "SORRY". "Z=0" means 
that the command/verb was not valid, or wasn't appropriate for the 
given sub-menu (e.g. "0" entered at the sub-menu for "GET" or "GO", 
etc).

213 PRINT"OK";GOTO 2

Line 213 prints out the message "OK.", and then jumps to Line 2. This 
is reached if the command for "USE" was valid, as well 
as "GET"/"DROP".

Line 301 through 320 do two things. First, each line corresponds to a 
room number (1 through 20, not surprisingly). Secondly, each line 
assigns valid exits from the present room (variable "A") via the "@
(x)" variable. Each "@" variable has one of 6 possible assignments:

1: @(1) = NORTH
2: @(2) = SOUTH
3: @(3) = EAST
4: @(4) = WEST
5: @(5) = UP
6: @(6) = DOWN

So, for example, in room #1 listed below, the player can move only 
SOUTH from the present room (IF A @(2)=2). SOUTH of Room#1 is Room#2 
(@(2)=2). Room descriptions are then printed out. 

If you have any questions on Lines 301 through 320, please e-mail me 
at: dunric@yahoo.com

301 IF A @(2)=2;PRINT"IN A TAVERN
302 IF A @(1)=1;@(2)=6;@(3)=3;PRINT"BY A WELL
303 IF A @(1)=4;@(4)=2;PRINT"IN A CHURCH
304 IF A @(2)=3;@(3)=5;PRINT"AT THE ALTAR
305 IF A @(4)=4;PRINT"IN STORAGE
306 IF A @(1)=2;@(2)=12;@(3)=7;@(4)=10;PRINT"NEAR A VILLAGE"
307 IF A @(5)=8;@(3)=11;@(4)=6;PRINT"BY A TREE
308 IF A @(3)=9;@(6)=7;PRINT"UP THE TREE
309 IF A @(4)=8;PRINT"IN A HUT
310 IF A @(3)=6;PRINT"AT A MOUNTAIN
311 IF A @(2)=13;@(4)=7;PRINT"IN A MEADOW
312 IF A @(1)=6;@(2)=15;PRINT"IN A FOREST
313 IF A @(1)=11;@(3)=14;PRINT"AT A CLEARING
314 IF A @(4)=13;PRINT"BY A LAKE
315 IF A @(1)=12;@(2)=16;PRINT"ON A BRIDGE
316 IF A @(1)=15;@(4)=17;PRINT"BY A CASTLE
317 IF A @(1)=18;@(3)=16;@(4)=19;PRINT"IN A HALLWAY
318 IF A @(2)=17;PRINT"IN A BEDROOM
319 IF A @(3)=17;PRINT"BY THE THRONE
320 RETURN
321 C=KP;C=C-48;Y=C;RETURN

Line 321 is the final line of the program. It waits for a keypress 
("C=KP", with "KP" being a reserved variable used by Bally BASIC to 
wait for a keypress), and then assigns the ASCII value now stored 
in "C" to a number 48 less than the present value.

In other words, "C=C-48" tells Bally BASIC to "assign an ASCII value 
48 *less* than what 'C' presently holds". So, if the ASCII value 
of "C" holds the number "1" (which is actually "49"), subtract 49 
from 48, to get "1". The ASCII values of 0 through 9 are: 48, 49, 50, 
51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, and 57, respectively.

Here's some harsh, but probably the simpliest, ways to save some memory for your program.  There's nothing amazing here...

>>
PRINTs out the title "BALLYVENTURE" on the screen.
>>

No title screen = 12 bytes saved just for the title itself, plus 4 more bytes for PRINT,"," and ;

>>
4 PRINT"@ COMMAND?
>>

Why not just reduce this to 4 PRINT"?"  That's another 8 bytes there.

>>
5 PRINT"1 GO 2 GET 3 DROP 4 USE
6 PRINT"5 FIGHT 6 INVENTORY
7 PRINT"7 LOOK 8 EXAMINE 9 QUIT
>>

Don't have a menu at all.  Show the menu at startup (in the load process--  not as part of the program) and be done with it.  Have the actions be part of the instructions.  This will save 70 bytes.  If you're looking to get the program into 1.8K, then quite a few sacrafices need to be made (as you've already noticed!).

>>
46 PRINT"1 NORTH 2 SOUTH 3 EAST
47 PRINT"4 WEST 5 UP 6 DOWN
>>

You won't need this menu at all either for the same reason as above.  This will save another 48 bytes.

So, if you make your program completely non-user friendly, you'll save 142 bytes.  This isn't really so hard a decision though; you need all of the memory that you can get.

1910:
FYI,

I've been working on adding "Professor Pacman" to the astrocade driver in
MAME.  This is probably the most sophisticated video hardware of any
astrocade chipset I've seen.  It is also used in the hybrid bowling/arcade
game "10-Pin Deluxe".

Basically, instead of only 16K of RAM as in the other commercial games,
there is a whopping 128K.  This is split into 4, 64K pages - this gives 4bit
planes instead of the normal 2.  The mapping from 2bpp to 4bpp is programmed
on the fly.  Only one page is visible at any time, however, you can select a
Read page and a Write page, independant of the Visible page.  Then, all
magic write operations take place using the read/write pages (I think).
Furthermore, I believe the blitter board (Pattern Transfer board) can be
used to copy regions from one page to the other this way.

Also, there is a 4096 color palette with 16 simultaneous colors, instead of
256 and 4 as in the other games (without the other color tricks).

Finally, when accessing a "write" page in memory, you can select one of four
"write modes" which affect how the data is used with respect to the
exisiting data.  They are overwrite (normal), xor, overlay, and underlay.
Color #0 is treated as transparent for to overlay and underlay modes.

I'm still hammering out all the details, but it's pretty neat to see such a
sophisticated system being driven by this same chipset.  I never really
expected to see something this fancy - I imagine it was really expensive at
the time (1983).

Thanks,
-Frank

> certainly when the first video ras cycle happens. And there are 40 of 
> these reads per line which means nothing extra is happening.

With 40 reads per line = 63.5 usec.  Therefore there are 64 rows (the
number of RAS address rows) read every 101.6 usec.  The refresh spec
on these RAMs is 64 reads every 2 msec.  This is how Midway (or, as we
used to call it, DimWay) could get away with buying DRAM refresh
fallout parts at a VERY good price).



> 
> The logic analyser traces show during the boot up menu 191 lines per 
> field of video ras cycles, each of which contains 40 reads. This 
> doesn't divide by 2, so I guess at least one line of dummy reads of

> number of screen refresh reads happen every field. Does anyone know 
> how many, what line they happen on and where the address comes from ? 
> Does the address chip latch the z80's refresh counter and use that ?

I doubt it.  My guess would be that the screen refresh counte (H and
V) generate screen refresh addresses outside active video just like
they do during active video.  These were hand-drawn customs, with a
minimum amount of automation.  There were no hardware description
languages available when these achips were designed.

AMI simply took the schematics from the PC board emulators, and
translated them to logic.  Then, they took the logic diagrams and had
Jeff Fredricksen and Terry Coleman verify that it did what the PC
boards did.

The easiest thing to do (and what certainly kept the gate count to a
minimum) would be to continue generating refresh cycles just like
during active video, and trash the data read.

The entire OS has functions which use a single register for passing in X coordinates.  In hires you've got 320 pixels to play with.  One 8-bit register won't cut it (this is probably why the NES 8-bit and other Japanese platforms liked to use 256 pixels horizontal res, even though this is not an even multiple of the color burst frequency).  Unlike consoles like the 2600, the Astrocade is chock full of built-in functions for everything game-related and it would be hard to write a game without them.  The OS is going to be pretty useless in hires mode and thus it will require writing all new graphics libraries from scratch.  I would guess that there is a hires OS with hires versions of these functions that were used in the coinop games.  At some point the coinop ROMs are going to have to be disassembled or the sourcecode dug up so we can figure this out.

Ultimately an FPGA arcade should probably have a toggle switch for hires that would swap out the OS with a hires OS or equivalent.  The OS area could all still be flashable but you'd decide which OS to bank in with the toggle.

1967:
Ok, I was taking a look at the Gorf driver in MAME, and discovered a bit of
a mystery.

Gorf uses the lightpen interrupt in a very strange way.  It has the lightpen
interrupt line tied to the "horizontal drive" line from the data chip.  So,
if you enable lightpen interrupts, you will get an interrupt every scanline,
at the beginning.  I think this is used as some kind of timer in gorf.

Ok - here's the really weird part.  The gorf code writes to bit 4 of port E
- and this is critical to the emulation working.  This bit has no documented
purpose in the Bally docs that I've seen.  So, I went back to the patent
drawing.  If you look on page 58 of the PDF, you will find the port E write
register marked as 1158a-e.  Sure enough, there are 5 bits connected there
(bit 0 through bit 4) instead of the 4 documented in the Nutting manual and
patent description.  (Bit 0 is 1158a, and Bit 4 is 1158e)

At first glance, it looks like bit 4 is the "force a lightpen interrupt
immediately" bit.  Maybe someone with a working console could try this out.
It would be interesting to see what happens.

-Frank
1968:
Ok - the rest of the story.  Bit 4 of port E is actually a "special"
lightpen interrupt enable bit.  Here is the difference:  The normal enable
(bit 1) will only allow lightpen interrupts inside a horizontal window -
from pixel 0-159 (or 0-358 in commercial mode).  The register normally reads
the pixel number +8 (or +16) in commercial mode.  If you use Bit 4 to enable
the interrupts - this window is gone.  You can get lightpen interrupts into
the horizontal overscan region - with actual values reading anywhere from 0
to the max - until you run into the bounds of your TV tube :).

Since Gorf is probably using this as a timer, they don't want the horizontal
window.

This would be a convenient way to measure the size of the overscan region,
for those of you with real lightpens :)

-Frank

As far as I can tell, no other programs make use of the Z-80 Mini-Course code.
